title: aham brahmasmi
tomorrow: 'I was Manu, and the sun.' a boast, or a fever?

segments.voice: Yesterday, aham brahmasmi beside a neighbor: I am, said first by Brahman and opened to whoever wakes; and I AM, God's own name, spoken to Moses. Today the week comes back.

Three little words. Take the saying apart and that's all it is. Aham, I. Brahma, Brahman. Asmi, am. Spoken aloud, the last two run together, brahmasmi, so the whole thing flows as one phrase: I Brahman am. So which of the three does the work? Every day this week leaned on a different one.
screen: `AHAM. BRAHMA. ASMI.` → `I BRAHMAN AM.` → `WHICH ONE DOES THE WORK?`

segments.voice: First, the I. The self alone said I am, and every name after it was added on: it's me, then the name. Then being alone, and the fear that came with it: fear comes from a second, and it left when no second was seen. An argument inside Advaita asked what practice does with the saying: build the knowing, or clear the way for what already is. Then three pictures of where the self is: a razor in its case, fire in the wood, the footprint everything is found by. Then what's dearest: the innermost self, dearer than a son or wealth, the one that can't be left on the curb. And yesterday, a neighbor's I AM beside aham brahmasmi, close in words and honestly different. So which word does the work? The text doesn't say, and readers differ on how to hear the whole. But in a sentence this short, none of the three stands alone. Take out the I and it's a statement about something far off. Take out Brahman and it's only a name tag. Take out am and nothing is claimed at all.
screen: `THE I, AND THE FEAR.` · `BUILD IT, OR SEE IT.` · `A RAZOR, A FIRE, A FOOTPRINT.` · `DEAREST, AND A NEIGHBOR'S I AM.` · then, large: `THREE WORDS THAT ONLY WORK TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Stand and take a slow walk, across the room and back. On one step think aham, on the next brahma, on the next asmi, and let the three words keep time with your feet. When you sit again, let them go.
Aham brahmasmi: three small words, I, Brahman, am, and the saying this whole week has circled.
Your line: aham brahmasmi, three words that only work together. A full week, well walked.

fork.setup: a floormate asks: 'so if you're Brahman, you can't ever be afraid or sad, right?' by this week's readings, what's honest?
options: even the self in the story was afraid; seeing no second ended the fear.
right: knowing the saying means never feeling anything hard again.
the saying is only for gods and sages, not for real people.
fork.reveal: the Brihadaranyaka's story starts with the self afraid, and it opens the saying to gods, sages and people alike.

original.note: Sanskrit brahma, the form of Brahman inside the saying; joined to asmi, it becomes brahmasmi.

trapdoor: what you thought: aham brahmasmi is one long mystic word.
what it means: three small words, aham, brahma, asmi: I, Brahman, am.
what a scholar hears: brahma and asmi join by sandhi into brahmasmi, a long a where the two vowels meet; asmi is the first person of the verb 'to be'.
recall: a second: where fear comes from
build the knowing, or see it
the footprint all is found by
